Type research · O'Neill Group

Sans serif, explained and shortlisted.

Eleven free sans serif typefaces, set in real O'Neill Group copy so the choice is made by eye rather than by name. Every face below is rendered in itself — what you see is what the brand would look like. No serifs anywhere in the recommendation, per the client.

10 August 2026 Prepared for Hunter, 10x Visuals 11 candidates · all free for commercial use

First, the word itself

A serif is a little foot. Sans serif means without them.

Serifs are the small strokes hanging off the ends of a letter — the feet on the legs of an R, the flick at the tip of a g. Sans is French for without. That is the entire distinction. Everything else is taste, and the client's taste has already ruled the left-hand box out.

Rg
Serif Marcellus — excluded

Feet on the R, a curled tail on the g. Reads as older, established, printed. Ruled out by the client, so it appears here once, as the thing being excluded.

Rg
Sans serif Libre Franklin — the recommendation below

Clean stroke ends, no feet. Reads as current, plain-spoken, and holds up at 13px on a phone. This is what you want carrying body copy, buttons and ad captions.

The constraint, and what it costs

Most brands run both — a serif for headlines because it carries weight, a sans for everything a person actually has to read. Ruling out serifs removes the easy source of contrast, so the hierarchy has to come from weight, size and letter-spacing instead of from a second kind of letter. That is a normal, disciplined way to build a brand; it just means the sans has to be strong enough to carry a headline as well as a paragraph. Every face below is judged on that.

The three kinds worth knowing

Sans serifs split into three families, and they say different things.

Once you can name these three, every font decision gets faster — you pick the family first, then the face inside it. Cutting across all three is how the stroke ends are finished: some faces cut them at a hard angle, others finish them soft and blunt. Given the objection to pointy shapes, the soft-ended faces are marked below.

Equity

Grotesque

Swiss-descended, neutral, no personality on purpose. Reads as institutional and factual. Think banks, airlines, Helvetica. Safe, sometimes anonymous.

Equity

Geometric

Built from circles and straight lines. Reads modern, friendly, start-up. Great for a logo, tiring in a long paragraph, and light on gravitas.

Equity

Humanist

Shaped by handwriting rather than a compass. Slightly irregular, warmest of the three, easiest to read at length. Civic, editorial, trustworthy.

The shortlist

Eleven candidates, set in the client's own words.

Same headline, same paragraph, same figures in every card, so the only variable is the typeface. The headline runs at the weight it would actually be used at, because with no serif in the system the sans has to hold the top of the page as well as the body. Ordered best to worst for this brand.

The recommendation

One family, three weights. Libre Franklin runs the whole system.

With serifs off the table, the cleanest answer is not to hunt for a second face — it is to stop at one and build the hierarchy out of weight, size and tracking. Single-family systems read as disciplined rather than sparse, which is exactly the impression the brand is selling, and there is no risk of two sans serifs sitting too close together and looking like a mistake. Below is that system running as it would on a landing page or an ad.

Putting it in

Three places it has to be installed.

  1. On your Mac, for graphics work

    Download the family from Google Fonts, unzip, select every file, double-click, Install. It then shows up in Photoshop, Illustrator, Canva desktop and Final Cut. The same place Poppins and Montserrat already live: ~/Library/Fonts.

  2. On the website

    One line in the page head, then set it as the body face. Works on WordPress, Elementor, Webflow and plain HTML alike.

    <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Libre+Franklin:wght@400;600;700&display=swap"> body { font-family: 'Libre Franklin', system-ui, sans-serif; }

  3. In the brand kit

    Record it the same way the colours are recorded: Libre Franklin Bold for headlines, mixed case, never all caps, tracked slightly tight at -0.025em. SemiBold for kickers, uppercase, tracked open at 0.18em. Regular for body. SemiBold with tabular figures for any rate, price or count. One face, four roles — anything beyond that and the restraint that sells the brand starts to leak. Write down that serifs are out too, so the next person to touch the brand does not helpfully reintroduce one.

Licensing — check before you widen the search

Every face on this page is under the Open Font Licence: free commercially, free to install, free to self-host, no attribution. The popular free foundry alternatives — Satoshi, General Sans and Switzer on Fontshare — are free for commercial use too, but their licence is reported to require written consent from the foundry before you self-host the webfont files. Fine for print and video, a question mark for the website, so confirm the current terms directly with Fontshare before specifying one for a client build.

Assumption to confirm

This is written against the Quiet Equity system on file for Brian O'Neill's Strategic Investing QLD — navy, gold, Marcellus and Inter. Two things follow that are worth confirming before this goes to the client. If O'Neill Group is a separate entity rather than a parent or rebrand of that one, the palette needs re-checking, though the eleven candidates and the family logic hold either way. And if it is the same brand, dropping serifs means retiring Marcellus — that is a live change to an existing identity, not just a choice of body face, and every asset already built on it would need reissuing.
